63: \begin{abstract}
64: Motivated by TeV-scale neutrino mass models, we propose a systematic treatment of heavy neutrino $(N)$ production at hadron colliders.
65: 
66: Our simple and efficient modeling of the vector boson fusion (VBF) $W^\pm\gamma\rightarrow N\ell^\pm$ and $N\ell^\pm+nj$ signal definitions
67: resolve collinear and soft divergences that have plagued past studies, and is applicable to other color-singlet processes, 
68: e.g., associated Higgs $(W^\pm h)$,  sparticle $(\tilde{\ell}^\pm\tilde{\nu_\ell})$, and charged Higgs $(h^{\pm\pm}h^{\mp})$ production.
69: 
70: We present, for the first time, a comparison of all leading $N$ production modes, 
71: including both gluon fusion (GF) $gg\rightarrow Z^*/h^*\rightarrow N\overset{(-)}{\nu_\ell}$ and VBF.
72: 
73: We obtain fully differential results up to next-to-leading order (NLO) in QCD accuracy 
74: using a Monte Carlo tool chain linking FeynRules, N{\small LO}CT, and MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO.
75: Associated model files are publicly available.
76: At the 14 TeV LHC, the leading order GF rate is small and comparable to the NLO $N\ell^\pm+1j$ rate;
77: at a future 100 TeV Very Large Hadron Collider, GF dominates for $m_N={300-1500}$ GeV, beyond which VBF takes lead.
78: \end{abstract}

87: \section{Introduction}\label{sec:Intro}
88: 
89: The origin of neutrino masses $m_\nu$ that are tiny compared to all other fermion masses is a broad issue
90: in particle physics, cosmology, and astrophysics.
91: Nonzero $m_\nu$ imply the existence of new particles~\cite{Ma:1998dn},
92: but more generally, physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM) that may be observable at current and future experiments.
93: Extended neutrino mass 
94: models~\cite{Pilaftsis:1991ug,Kersten:2007vk,Gu:2008yj,Dev:2009aw,Zhang:2009ac,Adhikari:2010yt,Chen:2013fna,Dev:2013oxa,Dev:2015vra} based on the
95: Type I~\cite{Minkowski:1977sc,Yanagida:1979as,VanNieuwenhuizen:1979hm,Ramond:1979py,Glashow:1979nm,Mohapatra:1979ia,
96: GellMann:1980vs,Schechter:1980gr,Shrock:1980ct,Schechter:1981cv}, 
97: Inverse~\cite{Mohapatra:1986aw,Mohapatra:1986bd,Bernabeu:1987gr}, and 
98: Linear Seesaw Mechanisms~\cite{Akhmedov:1995ip,Akhmedov:1995vm}, 
99: feature heavy mass eigenstates $N_{i}$ that couple to electroweak (EW) bosons via mixing with left-handed (LH) neutrinos $\nu_{L}$.
100: In these TeV-scale scenarios, active-sterile mixing can be as large as  $\vert V_{\ell N_i}\vert\sim10^{-3}-10^{-2}$, 
101: and consistent with oscillation and EW data~\cite{Atre:2009rg,Antusch:2014woa,deGouvea:2015euy},
102: as well as direct searches by the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments~\cite{Aaij:2014aba,Aad:2015xaa,Khachatryan:2016olu}.
103: Thus, if kinematically accessible, 
104: hadron colliders can produce heavy neutrinos that
105: decay to lepton number- and/or flavor-violating final states with observable rates.
106: 
107: 
108: 
109: For heavy $N$ masses $m_N$ above the EW scale, a systematic comparison of all leading single $N$ production modes cataloged 
110: in~\cite{Keung:1983uu,Datta:1993nm} has never been performed.
111: Most investigations focus on the charge current (CC) Drell-Yan (DY) 
112: process~\cite{Keung:1983uu,Pilaftsis:1991ug,Han:2006ip,delAguila:2006bda,delAguila:2007qnc,Atre:2009rg},
113: as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:diagrams}(a),
114: \begin{equation}
115:  q ~\overline{q'} \rightarrow W^* \rightarrow N ~\ell^\pm, ~\quad q \in \{u,c,d,s,b\},
116:  \label{eq:DYCC}
117: \end{equation}
118: and has recently been found to be subleading in parts of this mass regime~\cite{Hessler:2014ssa,Alva:2014gxa}.
119: Missing in most analyses is the gluon fusion (GF) channel~\cite{Hessler:2014ssa},
120: which proceeds at leading order (LO) through quark triangles in Fig.~\ref{fig:diagrams}(b),
121: \begin{equation}
122:  g ~g \rightarrow h^*/Z^* \rightarrow N ~ \overset{(-)}{\nu_\ell}.
123:  \label{eq:GF}
124: \end{equation}
125: Variants of Eq.~(\ref{eq:GF}) have been studied elsewhere~\cite{BhupalDev:2012zg,Batell:2015aha}.
126: Formally, GF is a finite next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD correction to the neutral current (NC) DY process
127: \begin{eqnarray}
128:  q ~\overline{q} \rightarrow Z^* \rightarrow N ~\overset{(-)}{\nu_\ell}.
129:  \label{eq:DYNC}
130: \end{eqnarray}
131: 
132: Recent analyses have investigated the sizable EW vector boson fusion (VBF) 
133: process~\cite{Dev:2013wba,Bambhaniya:2014hla,Alva:2014gxa,Deppisch:2015qwa,Ng:2015hba,Arganda:2015ija,Das:2015toa}:
134: \begin{equation}
135:  q_{1} ~q_{2} ~\overset{W\gamma+WZ~\text{Fusion}}{\longrightarrow} ~N ~\ell^\pm ~q_{1}' ~q_{2}',
136:  \label{eq:VBF}
137: \end{equation}
138: and subleading CC DY with $n\geq1$ QCD jets~\cite{Dev:2013wba,Das:2014jxa,Das:2015toa}:
139: \begin{equation}
140:  p ~p \rightarrow W^{*}+ nj \rightarrow N\ell^\pm+  nj, \quad p,j\in\{\overset{(-)}{q},g\},
141:  \label{eq:DYnj}
142: \end{equation}
143: but with conflicting results.
144: The last two processes are plagued by soft and collinear poles in $s$- and $t$-channel exchanges of massless gauge bosons, 
145: issues usually associated with perturbative QCD, and require care~\cite{Alva:2014gxa,Ruiz:2015zca}.
146: E.g., inadequately regulated diverges are responsible for the overestimated 
147: cross sections claimed in~\cite{Dev:2013wba,Das:2014jxa,Deppisch:2015qwa,Das:2015toa}
148: 
149: 
150: We introduce a treatment that resolves all these issues.
151: Our results have widespread implications for SM and BSM physics:
152: the prescriptions for Eqs.~(\ref{eq:VBF}) and (\ref{eq:DYnj}) are applicable to, among other processes,
153: associated Higgs $(W^\pm h)$,  sparticle $(\tilde{\ell}^\pm\tilde{\nu_\ell})$, and charged Higgs $(h^{\pm\pm}h^{\mp})$ production.
154: 
155: To date, our study is the most accurate and comprehensive presentation of heavy $N$ production mechanisms at colliders.
156: It represents the first time properties of infrared and collinear (IRC) safety have been so rigorously imposed in this context, particularly to VBF.
157: 
158: Furthermore, we obtain modest next-to-leading order (NLO) in QCD corrections, demonstrating the stability of our approach.
159: 
160: \begin{figure*}[!th]
161: \includegraphics[width=0.90\textwidth]{feynmanDiagrams.eps}
162: \caption{Heavy neutrino production via (a) charge (neutral) current Drell-Yan, (b) gluon fusion, and (c) $W\gamma$ fusion.}
163: \label{fig:diagrams}
164: \end{figure*}
165: 
166: We guarantee the perturbativity of the VBF process by factorizing and resumming the $t$-channel $\gamma$
167: into a DGLAP-evolved parton distribution function (PDF).
168: Using a $\gamma$-PDF, one considers instead, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:diagrams}(c),
169: \begin{equation}
170:  q ~\gamma \rightarrow N ~\ell^\pm ~q'.
171: \end{equation}
172: $WZ$ fusion is subleading and can be neglected~\cite{Alva:2014gxa}.
173: 
174: We regularize Eq.~(\ref{eq:DYnj}) by imposing transverse momentum $(p_T)$ cuts consistent with Collins-Soper-Sterman (CSS) 
175: $p_T$-resummation~\cite{Collins:1984kg}.
176: 
177: Our Monte Carlo (MC) framework allows us to compute fully differential Feynman diagrams up to one loop, 
178: and therefore GF at LO and the remaining processes at NLO;
179: only Eq.~(\ref{eq:DYCC}) has been evaluated before at NLO~\cite{Ruiz:2015gsa,Das:2016hof}.
180: 
181: 
182: 
183: At the 14 TeV LHC, the CC DY channel prevails for $N$ masses $m_N=150-850\GeV$; above this, the VBF cross section is larger.
184: However, due to the $gg$ luminosity increase, GF is the leading mechanism at a hypothetical future 100 TeV Very Large Hadron Collider (VLHC)
185: for $m_N = {300-1500}\GeV$; at higher $m_N$, VBF dominates.
186: 
187: 
188: We now introduce our theoretical model, computation procedure,
189: and signal definition prescription.
190: After presenting and discussing results, we conclude.

197: \section{Heavy Neutrino Model}\label{sec:Theory}
198: 
199: For  
200: $i~(m) =1,\dots,3$, LH (light) states and 
201: $j~(m')=1,\dots,n$, right-handed (heavy) states,
202: chiral neutrinos can be expanded into mass eigenstates by the rotation
203: \begin{eqnarray}
204: \begin{pmatrix} \nu_{Li} \\  N_{Rj}^c \end{pmatrix}
205: =
206: \begin{pmatrix} 
207: U_{3\times3} && V_{3\times n} \\
208: X_{n\times3} && Y_{n\times n}
209: \end{pmatrix}
210: \begin{pmatrix} \nu_{m} \\ N_{m'}^c \end{pmatrix}.
211: \end{eqnarray}
212: After rotating the charged leptons into the mass basis, 
213: which we take to be the identity matrix for simplicity,
214: $U_{3 \times3}$ is the observed light neutrino mixing matrix and
215: $V_{3 \times n}$ parameterizes active-heavy mixing. 
216: In the notation of~\cite{Atre:2009rg}, the flavor state $\nu_{\ell}$ in the mass basis is
217: \begin{equation}
218:  \nu_{\ell} = \sum_{m=1}^{3} U_{\ell m}\nu_{m} + \sum_{m'=1}^{n}V_{\ell m'} N^{c}_{m'}.
219: \end{equation}
220: For simplicity, we consider only one heavy mass eigenstate, labeled by $N$. This does not affect our conclusions.
221: The interaction Lagrangian with EW bosons is then
222: \begin{eqnarray}
223:   \mathcal{L}_{\rm Int.} = 
224:   &-& \frac{g}{\sqrt{2}}W^+_\mu		\sum_{\ell=e}^\tau \sum_{m=1}^3 ~\overline{\nu_m} ~U_{\ell m}^*	~\gamma^\mu P_L\ell^-\nonumber\\
225:   &-& \frac{g}{\sqrt{2}}W^+_\mu		\sum_{\ell=e}^\tau 		~\overline{N^c} ~V_{\ell N}^* 	~\gamma^\mu P_L\ell^-\nonumber\\
226:   &-& \frac{g}{2\cos\theta_W}Z_\mu	\sum_{\ell=e}^\tau \sum_{m=1}^3	~\overline{\nu_m} ~U_{\ell m}^*	~\gamma^\mu P_L\nu_\ell\nonumber\\
227:   &-& \frac{g}{2\cos\theta_W}Z_\mu	\sum_{\ell=e}^\tau 		~\overline{N^c} ~V_{\ell N}^*	~\gamma^\mu P_L\nu_\ell\nonumber\\
228:   &-& \frac{g m_N}{2M_W} h	\sum_{\ell=e}^\tau 		~\overline{N^c} ~V_{\ell N}^*	 P_L\nu_\ell + \text{H.c.}
229:   \label{eq:Lagrangian}
230: \end{eqnarray}
231: 
232: 
233: Precise values of $V_{\ell N}$ are model-dependent and are constrained by oscillation and collider experiments, 
234: tests of lepton universality, and $0\nu\beta\beta$-decay~\cite{Atre:2009rg,Antusch:2014woa,deGouvea:2015euy}.
235: However, $V_{\ell N}$ factorize in $N$ production cross sections such that
236: \begin{equation}
237:  \sigma(pp\rightarrow N~X) = \vert V_{N\ell}\vert^2 ~\times~ \sigma_{0}(pp\rightarrow N~X),
238: \end{equation}
239: where $\sigma_{0}$ is a model-independent ``bare'' cross section in which one sets $\vert V_{N\ell}\vert=1$.
240: Hence, our results are applicable to various heavy neutrino models.
241: 
242: 
243: 
244: \section{Computational Setup}\label{sec:MC}
245: 
246: We implement the above Lagrangian with Goldstone boson couplings in the Feynman gauge into FeynRules (FR) 2.3.10~\cite{Alloul:2013bka,Christensen:2008py}.
247: QCD renormalization and $R_2$ rational counterterms are calculated with \nloct~1.02 (prepackaged in FR)~\cite{Degrande:2014vpa} 
248: and FeynArts 3.8~\cite{Hahn:2000kx}.
249: Feynman rules are collected into a universal output file (UFO)~\cite{Degrande:2011ua} and is available publicly~\cite{nloFRModel}.
250: We obtain fully differential results using MadGraph5$\_$aMC$@$NLO  2.3.3~\cite{Alwall:2014hca}.
251: SM inputs are taken from the 2014 Particle Data Group~\cite{Agashe:2014kda}:
252: \begin{eqnarray}
253:  \alpha^{\rm \overline{MS}}(M_{Z})		&=& 1/127.940, \quad M_{Z}=91.1876\GeV, \nonumber\\ 
254:  \sin^{2}_{\rm \overline{MS}}(\theta_{W}) 	&=& 0.23126.
255:  \label{eq:smInputs}
256: \end{eqnarray}
257: We assume five massless quarks, take the Cabbibo-Kobayashi-Masakawa (CKM) matrix to be diagonal with unit entries,
258: and use the NLO NNPDF2.3 QED PDF (\texttt{lhaid:244600}) ~\cite{Ball:2013hta},
259: which features a $\gamma$-PDF with both elastic and inelastic components,
260: at collider energies of $\sqrt{s}=14$ and $100$ TeV. 
261: We extract $\alpha_s(\mu_r^2)$ from the PDFs.
262: 
263: 
264:

266: \section{Infrared- and Collinear-Safe Hadron Collider Signal Definitions}\label{sec:SigDef}
267: 
268: To consistently compare channels and colliders, 
269: we follow the 2013 Snowmass recommendations~\cite{Avetisyan:2013onh}
270: and evaluate cross sections assuming the same fiducial acceptance.
271: In practice, however, one tunes cuts to specific colliders and final states.
272: Jet and charged lepton pseudorapidities $(\eta^{j,\ell})$ and charged lepton $p_T$ are required to satisfy~\cite{Avetisyan:2013onh}:
273: \begin{equation}
274:  \vert\eta^{j,\ell}\vert < 2.5, \quad p_T^\ell > 20\GeV.
275:  \label{eq:LepCuts}
276: \end{equation}
277: QCD radiation in Eq.~(\ref{eq:DYnj}) gives rise to fixed order (FO) cross sections that scale as powers of $\log(Q^2/q_T^2)$:
278: \begin{equation}
279:  \sigma(pp\rightarrow N\ell^\pm+nj) \sim \sum^n_k \alpha_s^k(Q^2)\log^{(2k-1)}\left(\frac{Q^2}{q_T^2}\right).
280:  \label{eq:qcdPowerSeries}
281: \end{equation}
282: $Q\sim m_N$ is the scale of the hard scattering process
283: and $q_T \equiv \sum_k^n p_{T,k}^{j}$ is the $(N\ell)$-system's transverse momentum,
284: which equals the sum of all jet $p_T$.
285: 
286: The perturbativity of these logarithms for TeV-scale leptons was studied in~\cite{Ruiz:2015zca}.
287: In the CSS $p_T$-resummation formalism~\cite{Collins:1984kg}, FO results are trustworthy when
288: $\alpha_s(Q^2)$ is perturbative, with $\Lambda_{\rm QCD} = 0.2\GeV$, and $q_T$ is comparable to $Q$:
289: \begin{equation}
290:  \log\frac{Q}{\Lambda_{\rm QCD}}\gg1 \quad\text{and}\quad \log^2\frac{Q}{q_T}\lesssim\log\frac{Q}{\Lambda_{\rm QCD}}.
291: \end{equation}
292: 
293: Imposing $Q = m_N$, jets in Eq.~(\ref{eq:qcdPowerSeries}) must satisfy
294: \begin{equation}
295:  \sum_k^n p_{T,k}^{j} \gtrsim m_N \times e^{-\sqrt{\log(m_N/\Lambda_{\rm QCD})}}.
296:  \label{eq:cssPTBound}
297: \end{equation}
298: Taking for example $n=1$ and $m_N$ up to $1~(1.5)\TeV$, the mass range of interest at 14 (100) TeV, this translates to
299: \begin{equation}
300:  p_T^j \gtrsim 55~(80)\GeV.
301: \end{equation}
302: Weaker $p_T^j$ cuts lead to artificially large logarithms and overestimated cross sections in Eq.~(\ref{eq:qcdPowerSeries}).
303: 
304: We cluster jets with FastJet~\cite{Cacciari:2005hq,Cacciari:2011ma} 
305: using the anti-$k_T$ algorithm~\cite{Cacciari:2008gp} with a separation parameter of $ \Delta R = 0.4$.
306: For differential events, we parton shower (PS) with Pythia 8.212~\cite{Sjostrand:2014zea}.
307: 
308: 
309: We equate the factorization and renormalization scales
310: to half the sum over final-state transverse masses (\texttt{dynamical\_scale\_choice=3} in \mgamc):
311: \begin{eqnarray}
312:  \mu_f, \mu_r, \mu_0 = \sum_{k=N,\ell,\text{jets}}\cfrac{m_{T,k}}{2} = \frac12\sum_{k} \sqrt{m_k^2 + p_{T,k}^2}.
313: \end{eqnarray}
314: 
315: 
316: 
317: 
318: 
319: 
320: We quantify the scale dependence by varying it over
321: \begin{equation}
322:  0.5  \leq \mu/ \mu_0 \leq2.
323: \end{equation}

326: In our framework, the CC DY rate at NLO can be calculated via the \mgamc~commands:
327: \begin{verbatim}
328: > import model HeavyN_NLO
329: > define p  = u c d s b u~ c~ d~ s~ b~ g
330: > define j  = p
331: > define mu = mu+ mu-
332: > generate p p > n2 mu [QCD]
333: > output PP_Nl_NLO; launch;

335: Similarly, the inclusive NC DY at NLO is calculated by
336: \begin{verbatim}
337: > define vv = vm vm~
338: > generate p p > n2 vv [QCD]
339: > output PP_Nv_NLO; launch;
340: \end{verbatim}
341: and the inclusive CC $\DYj$ NLO rate by
342: \begin{verbatim}
343: > generate p p > n2 mu j QED=2 QCD=1 [QCD]
344: > output PP_Nl1j_NLO; launch;
345: \end{verbatim}

347: 
348: GF is a loop-induced process, which are only recently~\cite{Hirschi:2015iia} supported by \mgamc.
349: Such fully automated computations at NLO are unavailable since the two-loop technology does not currently exist.
350: We therefore perform the LO calculation matched and merged with up to one additional jet via the MLM scheme \cite{Mangano:2006rw}.
351: We discard loops that are actually virtual corrections to the DY process
352: and keep only diagrams where gluons do not appears in the loop.
353: The inclusive, unmatched LO GF rate can be calculated with
354:  \begin{verbatim}
355: > generate g g > n2 vv [QCD]
356: > output GGF_Nv_LO; launch;
357: \end{verbatim}
358: {Note that the $h^*/Z^*$ interference vanishes due to $C$-invariance/Fury's theorem
359: and the (anti-) symmetric nature of the residual $h~(Z)$ coupling~\cite{Willenbrock:1985tj,Hessler:2014ssa}.}

374: 
375: The difficulty in modeling $W\gamma$ fusion stems from the $t$-channel photon propagator, 
376: which, like Eq.~(\ref{eq:qcdPowerSeries}) for $N\ell^\pm+nj$, gives rise to logarithms of the form~\cite{Alva:2014gxa}
377: \begin{equation}
378: d\sigma(q_{1}q_{2}\rightarrow N \ell^\pm q_{1}' q_{2}') \sim 
379: \log\left(\cfrac{m_N^2}{M_W^2}\right)\log\left(\cfrac{m_N^2}{p_T^{j_\gamma 2}}\right).
380: \label{eq:VBFLogs}
381: \end{equation}
382: Here, $p_T^{j_\gamma}$ is the $p_T$ of the jet associated with the photon exchange.
383: However, consistent treatment of Eq.~(\ref{eq:VBFLogs}) dictates $p_T^j$ cuts excessive for $\gamma$-initiated processes. 
384: A resolution is to collinearly factorize and resum the photon piece into a DGLAP-evolved $\gamma$-PDF, consider instead
385: \begin{equation}
386:  q ~\gamma \rightarrow N ~\ell^\pm ~q',
387:  \label{eq:qaScattering}
388: \end{equation}
389: and evolve the PDF to the hard scattering scale.
390: One loses the ability to efficiently tag a second forward/backward jet but gains a large (logarithmic) total rate enhancement~\cite{Alva:2014gxa}.
391: Eq.~(\ref{eq:qaScattering}) is realization of the structure function approach to VBF~\cite{Han:1992hr}.
392: Formally, the $N\ell^\pm qq'$ channel can be recovered by performing the ACOT-like jet matching explicitly as in~\cite{Alva:2014gxa}
393: or evaluating the NLO in QED corrections to Eq.~(\ref{eq:qaScattering}).
394: For VBF, we impose the $\eta^{j},p_T^{j}$ cuts of~\cite{Alva:2014gxa}:
395: \begin{equation}
396:  \vert\eta^{j_\VBF}\vert < 4.5, \quad p_T^{j_\VBF} > 30\GeV.
397: \end{equation}
398: Collinear poles associated with $t$-channel $\ell$ exchange emerge in Eq.~(\ref{eq:qaScattering}) but are regulated by cuts in Eq.~(\ref{eq:LepCuts}).
399: The process at NLO in QCD is simulated by

401: > define q = u c d s b u~ c~ d~ s~ b~
402: > generate    q a > n2 mu q QED=3 QCD=0 [QCD]
403: > add process a q > n2 mu q QED=3 QCD=0 [QCD]
404: > output PP_VBF_NLO; launch;
405: \end{verbatim}

511: \subsection{NLO+PS Kinematics at 14 TeV}
512: We now consider the differential distribution for the processes in Fig.~\ref{fig:diagrams} but focus largely on the VBF channel.
513: 
514: The kinematics of heavy lepton production from DY currents at NLO and NLO+Leading Log(recoil) was studied in~\cite{Ruiz:2015zca}.
515: There, the differential NLO $K$-factors, defined as
516: \begin{equation}
517:  K_{\mathcal{O}}^{\rm NLO} \equiv \cfrac{d\sigma^{\rm NLO}/d\mathcal{O}}{d\sigma^{\rm LO}/d\mathcal{O}}
518: \end{equation}
519: for observable $\mathcal{O}$, were analytically shown to be flat in the leading regions of phase space.
520: In these regions, NLO contributions are dominated by soft initial-state radiation, which generically factorize for DY processes.
521: We confirm the flatness of $K_{\mathcal{O}}^{\rm NLOPS}$ for the DY channels, 
522: including for complex observables such as cluster mass in the $N\ell\rightarrow 3\ell \nu$ final state.
523: 
524: 
525: The phenomenology of the GF channel has not been previously studied.
526: It is beyond the scope of this investigation to do so here and will be presented elsewhere.
527: 
528: 
529: At $\sqrt{s} = 14$ TeV and representative  neutrino mass $m_N = 500\GeV$,
530: the LO distributions for the $W\gamma$ fusion process was studied in Ref.~\cite{Alva:2014gxa}.
531: 
532: For the first time, we show in Fig.~\ref{fig:vbfDifferential} the NLO+PS (dash) and LO+PS (solid)-accurate distributions with respect to 
533: (a,c) $p_T$ and (b,d) rapidity $(y)$ of the (a,b) $N$- and (c,d) $(N\ell)$-systems. $K_{\mathcal{O}}^{\rm NLOPS}$ is shown in the lower panel.
534: 
535: For the two system, but particularly the $(N\ell)$-system, we observe a net migration at NLOPS of events from the lowest $p_T$ bins
536: resulting in $K^{\rm NLOPS}_{p_T}<1$ for these bins. At high $p_T$, $K^{\rm NLOPS}_{p_T}$ quickly converges to unity from above.
537: 
538: In the rapidity distributions, we observe a similar, but more pronounced, migration of events from large $y$ to smaller values,
539: consistent with shifts to larger $p_T$.
540: 
541: The charged lepton $p_T$ and $\eta$ distributions (not shown) demonstrate little sensitivity to $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s)$ corrections.
542: However, as VBF is dominated by $\gamma\rightarrow \ell$ splittings~\cite{Alva:2014gxa}, 
543: one does not expect such sensitivity to QCD radiation until $\mathcal{O}(\alpha^2 \alpha_s)$.
544: 
545: Though numerically less significant, we find that the NLO corrections to the VBF distributions are qualitatively different than those of DY-like systems:
546: whereas differential $K$-factors for DY processes tend to remain flat and above unity,
547: QCD corrections for $W\gamma$ fusion tend to depopulate low-$p_T$/forward regions of phase space and populate high-$p_T$/central regions.
548: This results in $K$-factors both above and below unity.

568: \section{Summary and Conclusion}\label{sec:Conclusions}
569: 
570: The origin of light neutrino masses remains elusive.
571: Extended neutrino mass models predict the existence TeV-scale heavy neutrinos $N_i$ that may be discovered at current or future collider experiments.
572: 
573: We propose a systematic treatment of $N$ production mechanisms at hadron colliders, 
574: and provide instructions for building IRC-safe VBF and $N\ell^\pm+nj$ signal definitions.
575: The prescription remedies issues that have plagued past analyses,
576: and is applicable to a number of other SM and BSM processes.
577: We report modest NLO corrections, demonstrating the perturbative stability of our approach.
578: 
579: We present also the first NLOPS-accurate differential distributions for the $W\gamma$ VBF process.
580: We observe nontrivial differential $K$-factors below and above unity.
581: 
582: In a model-independent fashion,
583: we present for the first time a comparison of all leading single $N$ production modes at $\sqrt{s} = 14$ and $100$ TeV.
584: Fully differential results up to NLO in QCD accuracy are obtained through a MC tool chain linking FeynRules, \nloct, and \mgamc.
585: 
586: Associated model files are publicly available~\cite{nloFRModel}.

7: Structured schema for a FeynRules ``.fr`` model file.
8: 
9: This is the shared representation produced by Lagrangian extraction and consumed
10: by the ``.fr`` generator (render.py). Design principle: STRUCTURE the regular,
11: error-prone blocks (M$Parameters, M$ClassesDescription, M$GaugeGroups,
12: M$Information, IndexRange) so an LLM never hand-writes their Mathematica syntax,
13: and CARRY the irregular parts (Lagrangian algebra, mixing blocks, NLO
14: bookkeeping) as verbatim Mathematica strings.
15: 
16: All numeric fields are strings so exact FeynRules syntax survives untouched:
17: rationals like ``-1/3``, decimals like ``1500.``, scientific ``2.5*^-3``.
18: """

22: import re

28: # A verbatim numeric string: "-1/3", "1500.", "2.5*^-3", "Internal", "Automatic".
29: NumberStr = str
30: 
31: _OPEN = {"(": ")", "[": "]", "{": "}"}
32: _CLOSE = {v: k for k, v in _OPEN.items()}
33: 
34: 
35: def unbalanced(text: str) -> Optional[str]:
36:     """Why ``text`` has unbalanced brackets, or None when it is balanced.
37: 
38:     Mathematica strings ("...") and comments ((* ... *), nested) are skipped. An
39:     unbalanced verbatim string renders into a .fr that FeynRules stops reading
40:     with "Unexpected end of file" or "Invalid syntax", long after the schema
41:     said OK.
42:     """
43:     stack: List[Tuple[str, int]] = []
44:     i, n, depth = 0, len(text), 0
45:     while i < n:
46:         c = text[i]
47:         if depth:                                  # inside a comment
48:             if text.startswith("(*", i):
49:                 depth, i = depth + 1, i + 2
50:             elif text.startswith("*)", i):
51:                 depth, i = depth - 1, i + 2
52:             else:
53:                 i += 1
54:             continue
55:         if text.startswith("(*", i):
56:             depth, i = 1, i + 2
57:             continue
58:         if c == '"':                               # string literal
59:             i += 1
60:             while i < n and text[i] != '"':
61:                 i += 2 if text[i] == "\\" else 1
62:             if i >= n:
63:                 return "unterminated string literal"
64:             i += 1
65:             continue
66:         if c in _OPEN:
67:             stack.append((c, i))
68:         elif c in _CLOSE:
69:             if not stack or stack[-1][0] != _CLOSE[c]:
70:                 ctx = text[max(0, i - 30):i + 1]
71:                 return f"unexpected '{c}' at character {i} (...{ctx})"
72:             stack.pop()
73:         i += 1
74:     if depth:
75:         return "unterminated comment"
76:     if stack:
77:         c, j = stack[-1]
78:         ctx = text[j:j + 30]
79:         return f"'{c}' at character {j} is never closed ({ctx}...)"
80:     return None
